newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Russia wants UN council statement on Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Russia wants UN council statement on Afghanistan.

text.p: With Afghanistan's Taleban militia in control of the country's capital, Russia on Saturday wants the Security Council to warn factions about imposing a military solution and deplore the rebels' execution of a former president hauled out of the U.N. compound.
The council may discuss Afghanistan when it meets on the Middle East crisis on Saturday, but some diplomats believed no action would be taken until Monday.

A draft statement prepared by Russia expresses grave concern about the "scale and the intensification of the military confrontation in Afghanistan, including the seizure of the capital city of Kabul by the Taleban."
It also "expresses dismay at the brutal execution" by the Taleban of former President Najibullah and others who had been given asylum in the United Nations compound in Kabul.

Two years after their formation, the Taleban, a one-time band of Islamic student vigilantes, took over Kabul early on Friday, executed Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai, and proclaimed strict Islamic rule.
They seized both men from the United Nations compound in Kabul and strung them up on a tower at the gates of the presidential palace where thousands gathered to watch.

Najibullah led a Moscow-backed government in Afghanistan for six years and was ousted on April 16, 1992, by Moslem Mujahedeen, who refused to let him leave the country and join his family in India. He sought refuge behind the walls of U.N. headquarters in Kabul, an unwilling recluse.

The Russian statement warns against attempts to impose a military solution in Afghanistan, calls for the immediate cessation of fighting and for all Afghan leaders "to renounce the use of force, to put aside their differences and to engage in a political dialogue."
It also calls on all states to refrain from interfering in the internal affairs of Afghanistan and to help promote peace in cooperation with the U.N. mission there.

The Russian draft is strongly opposed by Pakistan, not a council member, for any criticism of the Taleban, which it supports. The United States was reported reluctant to issue anything until the situation clarified, diplomats said.

Earlier on Friday, a representative of Afghanistan's ousted government called on the world not to recognise any regime the rebels would create and accused Pakistan of supplying the Taleban with weapons.

Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai, Afghanistan's deputy foreign minister, said President Burhanuddin Rabbani and his advisers had retreated to the north of Kabul to Parwan and Kapisa provinces and were contemplating their next move.
Pakistan's U.N. ambassador, Ahmad Kamal, said the old government was finished, Gahfoorzai had no standing and that the Taleban was in complete control of Kabul.

He said that the Taleban militia's top leader, Mullah Mohammad Rabbani, had already named himself as head of the country's six-man Supreme Council, and appointed Mullah Mohammad Ghaus as his foreign minister.
Ghafoorzai maintained the government still had the capability to mount a military attack but would not do so in the capital where too many civilian lives were at stake.
